lions.headline: Lions, Vikings mic’d up video shows redemption arc for Jameson Williams
lions.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 01: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) catches a pass in the corner of the end zone for a game-winning touchdown during the fourth quarter of a regular season NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions on November 1, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

After a win, the Detroit Lions always release their own version of a “mic’d up” compilation from the game. Their “Sights and Sounds” videos are always worth your time, as they incorporate unique camera angles along with Dan Miller radio calls and mic’d up moments that you can’t get anywhere else.

This week’s episode detailing the Detroit Lions’ 19-15 win over the Minnesota Vikings is can’t-miss.

Obviously, it was an emotional game with Jack Campbell’s traumatic injury, and I think One Pride Productions does a good job covering that moment with grace and compassion while properly conveying the gravity and emotions of the moment.

One other aspect of the game they uncovered was a moment of redemption that may have gone overlooked. This week, Lions receiver Jameson Williams was mic’d up, and it captured a couple of very interesting moments. Williams was involved in two extremely critical plays in the game. The first was his biggest mistake of the afternoon.

It was the fourth quarter, and the Lions led 12-7. They had just gotten an emotional fourth-down stop on defense, and it was up to the offense to extend their lead and bleed some of the remaining 13 minutes of game time. Facing a third-and-inches, Jared Goff ran a QB sneak up the middle for a first down. But Williams had not properly reported as off the line of scrimmage, causing the refs to call illegal formation. Detroit would not convert the third-and-6, and they punted it back to Minnesota.

As he was coming off the field, dejected, Williams was met with a coaching staff that had a message for him:

“You owe us,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said.

“I know, I know, I know,” Williams replied.

The Vikings capitalized on Williams’ mistake, driving the length of the field to take the lead 15-12 with just under nine minutes remaining. That’s when Lions receivers coach Scottie Montgomery repeated the message to Williams.

“You owe us,” Montgomery said. “Go back, make a play. I know the frustration. It [redacted] sucks. But we know you’re in. So stay in, okay?”

“Yup,” Williams replied.

What ensued was one of the Lions’ most impressive drives of the season. Detroit went 69 yards on just seven plays, led by five rushes for 57 yards—all of at least 9 yards. The cameras show Williams blocking is ass off the entire time. And on the first snap of Detroit’s goal-line offense, Jared Goff pulled the rug out from underneath the Vikings defense with a play-action pass to a wide-open Williams.

As he sprinted toward the sideline following his game-winning catch, Williams reminded the staff of his redemption.

Campbell: “Way to pay us back! That’s what I’m talking about!”
Williams: “Hey! I owe you, don’t I? I owe you, don’t I?”

Then, to Montgomery:

Williams: “Hey! I owe you, don’t I?
Montgomery: “Let’s go!”
Williams: “I still owe you! I still owe you! Aw, yeah! Aw, yeah!”

It’s a great moment caught on tape by the One Pride Production crew. You can watch the entire video below:

lions.headline: Lions Week 9 preview: Breaking down Dolphins’ offensive, defensive schemes
lions.body:
Jul 28, 2026; Miami Gardens, FL, USA; Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley speaks to reporters after practice at Baptist Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will square off in Week 9, with the Lions looking to extend their three-game winning streak—and the Dolphins seeking their second win of the season.

“(Dolphins Head) Coach (Jeff) Hafley’s done a good job in his first year,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “A lot of similarities to—just reminds me a little of what we were when we came in. They’re young, they’re hungry, they’re active. They run, they hit, they hustle, they finish, try to play disciplined ball, and they’re playing that way.”

Let’s take a closer look at the Dolphins’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and scouting notes from their most recently viewed games.

Dolphins head coach: Jeff Hafley

Head coaching seasons: 1st in the NFL
NFL coaching seasons: 10th season (Dolphins, Packers, 49ers, Browns, Bucs)
Defensive coordinator: 2 seasons (Packers 2024-25)
Other coaching roles held: DBs coach, Head Coach Boston College (2020-23), DC at Ohio State (2019)
Influences: Robert Saleh (scheme); Greg Schiano (Xs & Os), Dave Wannstedt (leadership)
Coached under: Kyle Shanahan, Saleh, Schiano, Wannstedt, Matt LaFleur, Mike Pettine, and Ryan Day (OSU)
Lions coaching connection: Jim O’Neil (Lions safeties coach/Assistant head coach) was the Browns DC in 2014-15 and the 49ers DC in 2016 when Hafley was the DBs coach for both teams
Play caller: Yes

Offensive coordinator: Bobby Slowik

NFL coaching seasons: 13th season (Dolphins, Texans, 49ers, Washington)
Offensive coordinator seasons: 4th season (Dolphins 2025-present, Texans 2023-24)
Previous coaching positions: Passing game coordinator, pass game specialist, offensive & defensive assistant
Influences: Mike and Kyle Shanahan, Mike McDaniel, Matt Lafleur, Sean McVay
Coached under: Shanahan, Shanahan, McDaniel, and DeMeco Ryans

Offensive scheme

Passing game: Shanahan Spread
Running scheme: Outside zone
Scouting notes:

Shanahan Core principles: marry pass and run, Shotgun looks (52%), lean on play-action (26.6%, 11th in the NFL), bunch formations, screens, etc.

11 personnel (58%) is the primary staple

21 personnel (28%) – traditional FB usage

12 personnel (9.3%)

Blocking scheme balance: Outside Zone (24%), Man (20%), Inside Zone (14%), Power (12.5%), Puller (7%), Counter (7%)

Prefer to get downhill with RB Ollie Gordon, with electric RB De’Von Achane on IR (ACL)

Rushing yards per game: 123.3 (11th); Rush yards per play: 4.4 (11th)

Heavy reliance on explosive plays over consistency in the run game

Explosives: EPA per rush: -0.03 (10th); Explosive run plays: 16.7% (3rd); 10+ yard rushes: 26 (7th)

Consistency is low: Success rate: 38.7% (20th); DVOA rushing: 26th; Stuffed Rate: 20% (26th)

Passing game is not clicking; DVOA passing: 26th

Passing yards per game: 166.7 (30th)

EPA per pass: -0.16 (24th); Explosive passing game: 24th

Pressures allowed (7 games): 99 (16th); Pressure rate: 43.2% (31st); Time to pressure: 2.77 (27th)

Sacks allowed: 21 (21st); Sack rate: 10.3% (31st)

RPO/rollout/bootleg concepts with QB Malik Willis to buy time in muddy pocket

Dan Campbell on Dolphins offense:

“Offensively, they really have an athletic offensive line that’s got mass. They run a versatile scheme. (RB Ollie) Gordon is a heavy back. You give him a lane, and he can hit it, hit it with speed, build the speed, and that’s where he gets dangerous. You let him hit the line of scrimmage with any type of speed and any crease and he can go. […] There’s a ton of this eye candy and motions and cutting the defense off. It’s a good scheme and they run it well, screens, gadgets, play pass off of it. (QB) Malik (Willis)’s done a heck of a job with all that stuff. (WR) Malik Washington, they got young receivers outside that are growing, up and coming, growing. Washington is a good football player, plays in the slot, he can play outside and he’s also their punt returner. So, he’s pretty dynamic in that regard. Look, this is a hungry team and they’re playing good football.”

Defensive coordinator: Sean Duggan

NFL coaching seasons: 3rd season (Dolphins, Packers)
Defensive coordinator seasons: 1st season
Previous roles: LB coach, defensive assistant
Influences: Jeff Hafley, Matt LaFleur
Coached under: Hafley, LaFleur
Staff ties to Detroit: Joe Barry (Lions DC during winless season in 2008)

Defensive scheme

Base: 4-3 Wide-9, 1-gapping front
Coverage: Zone-heavy, split-safety/Cover-3
Scouting notes:

Stay in Base 43 defensive front 52% of the time

Play fast and attack with four

Blitzing percentages are low (23%, 29th in the NFL) and mainly on third downs

“Replacement” blitzing (blitz a linebacker, drop an edge into coverage)

Pressure comes from DL stunts and twists (almost all pressure)

Pressures: 77 (31st); Pressure rate: 35.6% (18th)

Sacks: 9 (30th); Sack rate: 4.25 (28th)

Two of their best three defensive games have come in the past two weeks

Week 4 vs. Vikings — Pressure rate: 37%; 4 sacks

Week 7 vs. Jets — Pressure rate: 46%; 2 sacks

Week 8 vs. Patriots — Pressure rate: 50%; 3 sacks

Pass defense is bad: Pass yards allowed per play: 8.3 ypp (32nd); EPA per pass allowed: 0.26 (32nd)

Zone coverage 80%; Man coverage (15%)  — man coverage always means Cover-1

Single-high: Heavy Cover-3 (33%) and Cover-1 (15%)

Two-high: Cover-6 (17.6%), Cover-4 (14%), and Cover-2 Zone (13%)

Subpackages (48%) mean three-safety/Big-nickel sets (47%); rarely in Dime (1%)

Pre-snap with two-high safety looks (56%)

Post-snap option to shift to single-high (44%) and drop one into the box

Safeties help in the run game — mostly middle of the League results

Rush yards allowed per game: 113.1 (16th); per rush: 3.8 (8th)

Vulnerable to explosive runs: 10.17% (17th); EPA per rush allowed: -0.06 (20th)

Success rate allowed: 41% (12th)

Dan Campbell on Dolphins defense:

“Defensively (DL Zach) Sieler is really the anchor in there. He’s played good football for a really long time. Smart, crafty, powerful, just can get an edge in the pass game. Active linebackers, with (Jordyn) Brooks and (Jacob) Rodriguez, football players. (CB Chris) Johnson’s done a heck of a job. Nickel corner, he’s pretty versatile in that regard.”

lions.headline: NFL trade deadline rumors: Lions, Bears could compete for same players
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears and Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions shake hands following the game at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The NFL trade deadline is coming soon (next Tuesday), and with such a tightly contested NFC North, there could be an arms race on the horizon. Currently the Minnesota Vikings lead the division at 6-1, but the 5-2 Detroit Lions and 6-2 Chicago Bears are close behind, and both teams are hunting to add more talent before Tuesday’s deadline. In fact, according to ESPN insider Dan Graziano, both the Lions and Bears could be hunting for the same players.

In one of his latest pieces for ESPN, Graziano said both the Lions and Bears have made calls about acquiring a cornerback.

“The Bears made their big move for [Jeffery] Simmons, but they’re still poking around on potentially available cornerbacks, as are the Lions,” Graziano wrote this week. “Detroit might also be in the market for help at linebacker, particularly in the wake of the terrible injury to mainstay Jack Campbell.”

It’s no surprise to hear that the Lions are still searching for a cornerback. The team admitted they were in the market for Joey Porter Jr. before he was eventually traded to the Dallas Cowboys. And the Lions’ cornerback situation hasn’t really changed since. While D.J. Reed is certainly playing better as the team’s No. 1 cornerback in recent weeks, Detroit is still seeking a No. 2 cornerback while rotating through the likes of Roger McCreary, Rock Ya-Sin, Khalil Dorsey, and Ennis Rakestraw.

The Bears, who already made a big trade deadline move by sending two first-round picks and more to the Titans for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, have also dealt with some issues in the secondary. No. 1 cornerback Jaylon Johnson is currently ranked 103rd out of 106 qualifying cornerbacks in PFF coverage grade (32.1), while CB2 Malik Muhammad isn’t faring much better (52.5, 78th).

At this point, it isn’t clear which cornerbacks are available to acquire at the trade deadline. But some of the more commonly thrown around names are Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen, Commanders cornerback Mike Sainristil, Dolphins cornerback JuJu Brent, and Chargers cornerback Donte Jackson. A month ago, we also compiled a list of defensive backs that the Lions could target at the trade deadline.

We’ll see if either team can pull off a move with just days remaining before the deadline.

michigan.headline: No. 16 Michigan vs. No. 4 Connecticut Preview: A reloading rematch
michigan.body:
The Connecticut Huskies will always be remembered fondly in Ann Arbor as the team the Michigan Wolverines took down to earn their first national championship in almost 40 years. Last April’s title game was not the prettiest sight — that is, until the confetti began to fall on one of the most dominant rosters in the sport this century.

Those Wolverines are a closed chapter, however, meaning the championship game rematch this Friday will look very different. The same is somewhat true for the Huskies, though there is nothing too foreign about entering the season in the top five and eying a return to the Final Four (as seemingly is the case every year). So early in the year, this game is far from make-or-break, but absolutely will impact seeding conversations for both teams in March.

Even more tangibly, this game is a quintessential early measuring stick for these reloaded rosters. Dan Hurley has built this program into the country’s best this decade, and the Huskies will be ready for revenge in a not-so-neutral location. Meanwhile, Mike Boynton faces the first big test of his tenure, where he will show just how close, or far, his squad is from competing with the top of the sport.

No. 16 Michigan (1-0) vs. No. 4 Connecticut (1-0)

Date & Time: Monday, Nov. 2, 6 p.m. ET
Location: TD Garden, Boston, MA
TV/Streaming: TNT

The last time these two teams met…needs no reminder. Only eight Wolverines logged minutes in the final, with just three of them remaining in college. Elliot Cadeau was 5-for-11 with a couple assists, hitting the first of Michigan’s two shots from deep. Trey McKenney famously hit the other, but was just 2-for-9 on the night, though he did snag eight rebounds. Roddy Gayle had a powerful putback dunk at the end of the first half, then drained out the clock with his heads-up heave of the ball in the season’s final seconds.

Which newcomers will stand out most?

In Indianapolis, Michigan leaned on the Yaxel Lendeborg-Morez Johnson-Aday Mara trio to anchor both ends of the floor, and now turns to JP Estrella and Moustapha Thiam, who are solid players but clear downgrades as of this moment. For UConn, Duke transfer Nik Khamenia and Seton Hall transfer Na’jai Hines will be the ones attempting to replace Alex Karaban and Tarris Reed, respectively.

Without Thiam, Estrella was the feature inside against Oakland and certainly looked the part, posting a double-double. Though it was one game, against a mid-major, Quinn Costello also threw his hat in the ring as a newcomer to watch. The path to victory for the Wolverines this year will involve more outside shooting, and the sharpshooting freshman was not afraid to let it go from deep, taking 10 threes against the Grizzlies, hitting 30 percent of them.

Both Khamenia (14 points, 6 rebounds) and Hines (12 points, 12 rebounds) transitioned smoothly onto their new team on Monday as well. While all of the incoming players and complementary pieces will certainly be a factor, Friday’s showdown could end up a McKenney-Braylon Mullins battle, with the returning offensive weapons shooting early and often in their respective season openers.

How will this offense attack UConn?

Even though the Huskies are typically stout in the paint, I do see the Wolverines giving Thiam and Estrella plenty of looks near the hoop. However, given that the continuity of this team comes from the backcourt, this does feel like a game where Boynton is going to lean on Cadeau and McKenney to a large extent. Maybe this means Cadeau driving and setting up his bigs, but I also expect plenty of jumpshots as well.

It would be great if Thiam could be a huge factor in Boston, though this is an extremely tough game to make a debut. From rebounding to shot blocking to being a target for the guards, Boynton will need the big man to be involved in all areas as much as he can. UConn has been amongst the top 10 teams in two-point defense each of the past five years; this is a great early test for Thiam against a physical interior.

UConn dominated Gardner Webb on Monday, which says absolutely nothing, as the Runnin Bulldogs project to be one of the worst teams in the entire country. Still, one thing to always watch with Hurley’s squad is tempo, as the Huskies’ offense will be very methodical, leading to opponents getting frustrated with the ball themselves. Michigan must be patient and find the right look, as chucking up threes did not work so well in the opener.

Can the defense stand its ground?

The national championship squad was built on a ridiculous two-point differential that featured the second-lowest two-point accuracy by opponents (on the fourth-farthest average distance), while the Michigan offense was the exact opposite. There is going to be a dropoff in this department on both ends of the floor, but rim protection is something to keep an eye on early.

Performances over the preseason showed a heavy regression when it came to defending twos (including an influx of fouls), and while this was not the end of the world against Oakland, UConn offers patience and ball movement that often ends up in a quality look. There is no Mara to worry about in the paint on Friday, putting a lot of pressure on Thiam, and even Estrella and Reed, to make things difficult inside.

As good as Mullins and Silas Demary (and Khamenia) can be from range, it is the interior defense I am most curious to see. The personnel is different, but I think back to how Duke kept winning inside last February, especially when it came to rebounding. Michigan obviously was fine against UConn in April, but do not expect a defensive performance to that level given what we have seen so far.

michigan.headline: Michigan State at Michigan Preview: Paul Bunyan’s disappointment
michigan.body:
No one realistically expected Pat Fitzgerald to turn the Michigan State Spartans around in Year One. The Michigan Wolverines were forced into a coaching search, which theoretically gives Kyle Whittingham some cushion. Yet despite these differing circumstances, neither fanbase is overjoyed after a couple months under a new regime, as both rivals are under .500 in conference play.

Bystanders wondered if this rivalry was getting too toxic, with the animosity on fullest display during the 2022 tunnel incident. Well, perhaps the solution was having both programs bottom out, as neither is playing with the fire of before. Objectively, this game simply feels much more important — to both sides — when Michigan has something to play for.

But now, here we are. Michigan is ostensibly playing for a bowl, while State is playing for pride, as usual. Both coaches are getting their first taste of the rivalry and surely have had this date circled on the calendar, but the excitement on this game is severely muted when both teams are so out of the national picture. A loss would be terrible, so the Wolverines will need to show up, but this rivalry has seen better days.

Michigan State (2-6, 0-5) at Michigan (5-3, 2-3)

Date & Time: Saturday, Nov. 7, 7:30 p.m. ET
Location: Michigan Stadium, Ann Arbor, MI
TV/Streaming: Peacock

The Wolverines have taken four straight in this rivalry, though in two very different varieties. 2022 and 2023 featured future Big Ten champions that took care of business, allowing a combined seven points. The next two years were much uglier contests, with only the 2025 Michigan team ranked (just barely, at No. 25) amongst the four squads. Interestingly (annoyingly?), all four of those games were played at night as well.

Offense: Take it and run

It may just have been Rutgers, but Tommy Carr did everything fans have been longing for from a quarterback last weekend: 22-for-27 passing, 266 yards through the air, 54 more on the ground, three total touchdowns. There still are some missed passes (e.g. deep shots to Andrew Marsh), but the offense seems to finally be clicking, especially with Carr’s legs.

Everyone else’s legs, however, are apparently not trustworthy. This speaks way more to Jason Beck than the backs themselves, but the Wolverines are 98th in rushing yards per game and 112th in YPC with no reprieve in sight. The 3.58 YPC against an abysmal run defense was probably the final straw for any hope that Beck will make real changes, and the fact that much of that production came from Carr scrambles speaks volumes.

Run defense has been a calling card for the Spartans — and Fitzgerald — but this year has been unconvincing, ranking just 79th in YPC. Though the secondary ranks worse, relatively, on the season (91st in YPA), Big Ten opponents have found success in both avenues, with Nebraska, Wisconsin, and Illinois combining for eight passing touchdowns and then Northwestern and UCLA rushing for five scores the past two weeks.

For the Wolverines, I think this just means leaning into whatever is working. Carr was more clinical than lethal, but at this point the mid-range passing game seems more effective than the run game, which is a wild thing to say. I know SP+ still puts the State defense (No. 68) ahead of the Michigan offense (No. 87), but hopefully the quarterback change is enough to make this more of a toss-up.

Defense: The one good unit

Michigan offense: bad. Michigan State defense: mediocre. Michigan State offense: bad. Michigan defense: elite. That might be the story of how this game goes, as the Wolverines should be able to score (at least a little), but the same cannot be said for the Spartans. Perhaps Michigan’s odd defensive performance last weekend gives the State offense a little bit of hope, though it mostly felt like just a couple unfortunate plays against Rutgers.

State is bottom-10 nationally at 3.14 YPC with little success outside of the win over Eastern and that strange overtime defeat to Illinois. Cam Edwards actually started pretty well, but got injured in September and is now out for the year. That put Jaziun Patterson as the top back, but he too got hurt, leaving Kenneth Williams as the main option against UCLA (17 rushes, 54 yards).

Meanwhile, quarterback Alessio Milivojevic also missed the UCLA game and his alternates threw for a combined 109 yards against the Bruins, combining for one touchdown and two interceptions. While Milivojevic did have two of his better outings in his most recent games, the sophomore is not an intimidating presence and is not a threat with his legs, and his questionable status might mean his production is limited if he does play.

This is a long-winded way of saying that State has some health issues on offense, which in all likelihood does not even matter. The Michigan defense is far and away the best of the four units in this game, to the extent that this is likely the group that will singlehandedly insure the outcome. Trick plays and scripted drives are not enough to overcome this imbalance.

Rotten starts

Fitzgerald has reset the panic clock in East Lansing, with the fanbase willing to be patient as the program tries to climb its way back to the middle of the conference. Obviously, six straight losses (and counting) is never a great thing, but after the Jonathan Smith era, I suppose this transition cost is acceptable for the first season under the new regime.

Whittingham has somehow raised the panic level, despite Michigan’s coaching transition coming completely involuntarily. It is hard to believe that just three seasons ago this program was on the top of the sport; now it is hardly a factor in the playoff conversation. The veteran coach has made some questionable decisions thus far — primarily off the field — and this fanbase is hard to satisfy.

All of that being said…I would still much rather be Michigan. As bad as this season has been, the Wolverines are clearly a better football team than the Spartans. Relative to expectations, the conversation splits, but I still think that Michigan fans will be the happier ones at the end of the year. That statement will not be true, however, if the Wolverines stumble this Saturday. That makes this game meaningful even if every other circumstance points to it not being so.

michigan.headline: Fee Fi Foe Film: Michigan State Defense 2026
michigan.body:
Fee Fi Foe Film: Michigan State Defense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 6th, 2026 at 8:20 AM

Previously: Michigan State Offense
Well, this might end up being one of the shorter FFFFs I've ever done. The Michigan State defense lays in tatters, ravaged by injuries to the point that it's unclear what remains of this unit after the bye week. We will do our best today to parse through the injury report and the film to see what hope the Green & White have of performing
The Film: Due to the injury situation, I had no choice but to go with the most recent game, against UCLA just before MSU's bye week. Though UCLA's offense is vastly better coached than Michigan's, the injury to Nico Iamaleava has left the Bruins with a wobbly QB situation, so it isn't the worst comparison of all time. I am also going to take a look at the tape from the Illinois game to see what it looked like when an opponent hung 30+ on the Spartans.
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

Well, here we go with all the injuries. The Spartans have a defensive line that is down its most impactful player, as DT Ben Roberts went out with injury on the first play against UCLA and will be out against Michigan. That's a massive loss, as the other defensive tackles are a step down of several orders of magnitude and they were paved against the Bruins as a result. DT Eli Coenen was the other starter next to Roberts and has not been great this season. The backups, Mikeshun Beeler and Derrick Simmons didn't look much better to me, though the PFF grades are more average than bad. The injury also thrusts Carlos Hazelwood into the two-deep, logging 21 snaps vs. UCLA, and he couldn't play at all at this level of football.
So, that's grim. The defensive end spot is healthier but doesn't jump out me as terribly impactful. NC State transfer Kenny Soares Jr. and Weber State transfer Keahnist Thompson are the starters and they are okay fine. Anelu Lafaele began his career at Wisconsin but was on the MSU squad a year ago and he joins the other two to eat up most of the snaps at EDGE. All three are competent but not stars to me. Of the trio, I think I like Soares the most due to his pass rush chops, accumulating 24 pressures on the season and I gave him the Dangerman designation (though Lafaele has been grading out well there too).
At linebacker, MSU stomached a big blow earlier this season in the loss of Jordan Hall for the season. He projected to be one of the best players on this defense and was going to be the heartbeat of it at the MIKE spot. In his absence, Dion Crawford, a Buffalo transfer, has stepped up and has done well to pick up some of the slack. Unfortunately, WILL Cam Stodghill (Albany transfer) has not been as sharp and is a problem spot on this defense, popping up with poor run fits and tackling in the UCLA game. Auburn transfor Caleb Wheatland and SAM Brady Petzlaff played in the UCLA game as well and were not particularly impressive.
In the secondary, further injuries have complicated the picture. MSU was happy to be getting Charles Brantley back from his trial at Miami. A player so old he intercepted Cade McNamara in the 2021 Michigan game, Brantley was supposed to be a good CB1 and a veteran leader but Brantley underperformed and now is injured. He was starting alongside Tre Bell at outside corner, who was middling and is also injured.
Without their two starting corners, MSU is forced to turn to one-time Eastern Illinois transfer NiJhay Burt and more concerningly, freshman Jeremiah Favorite. Burt is okay and was not targeted much against UCLA but Favorite, like Hazelwood at DT, is a player who should not be on the field at all. That he has to start is a sign of how rough of a situation they are in. The nickel is Michael Richard, a Louisiana Tech transfer who has some responsibilities in the box as a run defender and feels like a replacement level player at the moment. Tyran Chappell is the first corner off the bench, I suppose, but I don't have much to say about him.
Finally, at safety, MSU is hoping that FS Devin Vaught will be able to go tomorrow night (he's listed as questionable). Vaught could've been the Dangerman for this piece but I didn't want to pick another player who might end up missing the game with that label. The Maine(!) transfer has been a stout run defender and has an interception on the season, providing some support to the embattled corners. SS Nikai Martinez is one of the oldest names on this defense, a returner from the Jonathan Smith era who I liked back in 2024 before he missed most of 2025 with injury. Martinez hasn't been as sharp this season but he and Vaught at least give some reliability to the safety room. Aveon Grose (Angelo's little brother) is the #3 safety but if Vaught can go, it'll be him and Martinez at this spot.
[AFTER THE JUMP: what remains of this defense]

Base set: Defensive coordinator Joe Rossi is a holdover from Jonathan Smith, retained by Pat Fitzgerald after he arrived in East Lansing and Rossi worked for PJ Fleck before that. He's tried and true #B1G. That also means I've charted Rossi's defenses a bit and they are usually aligned in a 4-2-5 look:

Last year MSU was using SAM Darius Snow to go 4-3 quite a bit, whereas this year against UCLA such looks generally just came from sliding the nickel inside, either in the box like a LB:

Or down on the line, as if it were 5-2:

There was also this goal line look:

That's most of what I had on formations in this game.
Man or zone coverage: Rossi has always been a guy running multiple coverages in my time charting his defenses. We first chronicled him at Minnesota in 2023, when it was a mix of quarters, Cov1, Cov2, Cov3, shifting around from snap to snap. In 2025 he was running Match Quarters and Pattern Match, showing quite a bit of Dantonio press quarters. Some dimensions have changed with Rossi, as Fitzgerald, a defensive coach by trade, has become his boss, but the coverages against UCLA were firmly in the zone category, as they have typically been.
Pressure: Speaking of Fitzgerald changing the equation, I do think that may have shifted things with regards to pressure. After being very blitzy at Minnesota in 2023 (37.5% of snaps!), the blitz numbers sat around 28% in his two seasons under Jonathan Smith. In this year's game against UCLA, it was a very un-blitzy 20%, and that was bolstered by a lot of run blitzing on the final drive, where UCLA was simply aiming to kill the clock. It was a lot of four man rushes and fairly vanilla ones at that. MSU rushed three only 5% of the time, meaning on three quarters of the snaps, it was a good old fashioned four man rush (usually of the DL).
Dangerman: This wasn't easy because coming into the year, I would've expected this section to be about either Charles Brantley or Jordan Hall. They're both injured, though Brantley wasn't playing well enough to earn it anyway. At the midway point of the season, I would've expected the Dangerman to be Ben Roberts. Now he's injured too. So who is left to pick from? There were a couple of choices but the player I liked the most who I am sure will actually play in the game is EDGE Kenny Soares Jr., the second consecutive year in which I've tabbed a Spartan EDGE after David Santiago a year ago.
Soares is one of the more lukewarm Dangerman picks of the year but we're dealing with a defense that has both hands tied behind its back in the way of talent. Thus, with Soares I was choosing someone who has had some moments on the season. UCLA didn't pass it much in the game I charted and when they did, the Spartans weren't generating much in the way of pressure. However, this pressure by Soares was one of the few positive moments in that game:
EDGE #1 to the bottom

He also teamed up with LB Caleb Wheatland for a pressure that forced an incompletion here:

On the season, Soares has a team-leading 24 pressures, ten more than any other player on the team, and his two sacks ranks second on the squad. Here was a near-sack from the Notre Dame game, that Tommy Carr's big bro somehow escaped from:

Not great tackling, I know, but I liked showing a play in which Soares was able to beat a tackle on a national title contending team. Soares has dropped into coverage 41 times on the year, per PFF's charting, and has an interception, which was a sweet, acrobatic play:

These highlights might not be thrilling or dazzling, but I had a limited selection of players to choose from. Soares is a guy who sometimes makes plays for an MSU defense that has lost almost all of their typical playmakers. In this sort of piece, he was the best I had to offer you.

Overview
Despite the injuries, if there's one thing I can say about MSU's defensive results it's "consistency". Though the formula week to week changes in terms of how the yards are obtained, all six power conference opponents have gained between 5.0 and 6.0 YPP on the MSU defense this season. None of them have gained more than 443 total yards and none of them have gained fewer than 360 total yards. Those opponents have scored 27, 31, 31, 38, 24, and 28 points, a tight range of two touchdowns between 24 points allowed and 38 points allowed.
The game I charted against UCLA was a window into the issues that MSU may have on their hands as a run defense with Ben Roberts injured. The DT had an 84.8 run defense grade per PFF and most MSU opponents save for Wisconsin had been held in check on the ground. But then Roberts went down on the first play from scrimmage and after that, it was demolition time. The Bruins never had much of an effective passing game with their backup QB starting, but it didn't matter because this was ugly. Right from the start, UCLA was earning easy wins on the ground by paving the defensive tackles, on this play Eli Coenen and Derrick Simmons:

And then it continued the entire rest of the game. Watch Mikeshaun Beeler get pancaked on this touchdown:

The number of problematic clips I have to show you is seemingly endless:

Though it was mostly on the defensive line, there were problems with the run fits too, like this from Caleb Wheatland and Cam Stodghill:

Of course, the brutal performance by the DL on that play is the source of the issue, but it goes from bad to worse due to the second level, where they miss Jordan Hall at LB. It's not to say that everything was bad, as there were some run stuffs, like this one:

But still, the situation from a personnel standpoint and what I saw on tape against UCLA (245 yards on 48 carries(!!) for 5.1 YPC) is such that if this were still Jim Harbaugh or Sherrone Moore's Michigan team, I would be sitting here saying "Michigan will just run it 50 times and smoke these guys, not even bothering to pass". Unfortunately, the realities of where things are at with the team under Kyle Whittingham's watch means we need to pivot and actually talk about pass defense.
Other teams to face MSU this season had more of their success through the air. Notre Dame had a decent but unspectacular rushing day against the Spartans but possible NFL QB CJ Carr was 18/24 for 234. Likewise, Nebraska rushed for only 3.8 YPC but Anthony Colandrea was 15/27 for 212, 7.9 Y/A with 2 TD and 0 INT. Ex-Spartan QB Aidan Chiles had a chaotic statline, 18/27 for 226 yards, 0 TD and 5 sacks (lmao).
The UCLA game was somewhat instructive to chart because the Bruins attempted 31 passes and definitely leaned on their run game, which I think will be Michigan's approach to this game. I wasn't enthused with the amount of pressure that MSU got, even if they've been better at it in other games. Though the team only has 12 sacks, Sparty actually grades out pretty well in team pass rush grade (not sure I agree, but they have over 100 pressures FWIW). Soares is a useful piece, as I pointed out, and one of the other ends, Anelu Lafaele, has had his moments too. When MSU gets pressure, it can make a difference, like the tandem of Falaele and Beeler getting pressure in the Illinois game to force an INT:

All this said, I don't view any of these rushers as terrors that Michigan must be prepared for. In which case, we can move on to talking about the coverage. The vulnerability I saw in MSU's pass defense in the UCLA game was mostly coming over the middle of the field, where neither Stodghill nor Dion Crawford are grading out well in coverage:

The other weakness in coverage is Justin Favorite, a freshman from South Carolina who ranked outside the top 1300 players in the 2026 recruiting class and should not be on the field right now. Injuries have caused that and Michigan should target whichever of Buchanan/Marsh are matched up against him relentlessly. Favorite was hit with a DPI in the UCLA game and then got beat over the top for a deep ball TD:

He's not ready and if Michigan has any ounce of game-planning at all (questionable), that should be a focal point of said hypothetical gameplan.
I do want to shout out FS Devin Vaught, who may or may not play in this game. It would be another big blow for MSU if he can't go, as you'd probably be elevating career reserve Aveon Grose into his place. That's a stepdown, because Vaught has been a pleasant performer. He delivered a PBU here:

Vaught can't do it all and the secondary even with him playing (and before the injuries to Brantley/Bell), this group ain't the Legion of Boom, as the passing numbers show. Combing through other games, you see coverage busts like this:

One last topic: scrambling. After last week's game against Rutgers, Tommy Carr's legs now have to be taken seriously as a key source of offense for this Michigan team. I saw opportunitites to scramble from both games I looked at, since neither opposing QB were viewed as enough of a run threat to spy them. So, opportunities like this are probably on the menu:

If Carr does it enough, then I have to assume Rossi will adjust and build the defense around it. But wanted to acknowledge it as part of this scouting report.

What does this mean for Michigan?
If everyone were healthy, I don't think this is a bad defense. Not talented enough to be a good one, but it had enough impactful players and a coaching structure in place with Fitzgerald/Rossi to expect acceptable results. But week after week, different parts of the car have fallen off the car and what we're left with is a rickety vehicle just puttering along down the road. What's remaining now is a group that is there to be taken advantage of, a relatively untalented group with several screaming weaknesses at corner and defensive tackle.
Will that matter for Michigan? Who the hell knows! The Wolverines are had a "better" week on offense against Rutgers in that they scored 28 points, but the Scarlet Knights have one of the worst defenses in the country. Though this MSU group isn't sitting pretty, they are not a joke of a unit like Rutgers. I'd like to think that MSU's defensive tackles could be exploited for a productive ground day, but Rutgers' run defense is terrible and Michigan couldn't get much of anything going beyond Tommy Carr scrambles. There's a world where the ineptitude of Jason Beck and the Michigan offense allows MSU to keep them contained and this game turns into an ugly, grinding slogfest. But a better offense should be able to punish the Spartan D, because it really isn't a challenge to fear.

michigan.headline: Roundtable: Michigan Football vs Michigan State
michigan.body:
Oct 25, 2025; East Lansing, Michigan, USA; Michigan Wolverines quarterback Bryce Underwood (19) reacts after scoring a touchdown against the Michigan State Spartans during the first half at Spartan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brendan Mullin-Imagn Images | Brendan Mullin-Imagn Images

The Michigan Wolverines return to The Big House this weekend to take on their in-state rivals, the Michigan State Spartans. In this week’s Roundtable, Maize n Brew staff members give some takeaways from last week’s game, some bold predictions for tomorrow’s game and more!

As always, let’s reflect on last week’s game. Provide any takeaways you had from the Rutgers game.

Von: That was WAY too close for comfort. The offense actually put together a solid game from start to finish, but it was the defense and special teams that made the game at Rutgers be much closer than it should have been. Giving up an 80-yard touchdown pass to Rutgers is embarrassing enough, but to let that happen against its backup quarterback? Come on, man. As far as special teams go, Trey Butkowski is broken after missing four of his last six field goals. These types of things should not be happening on a Kyle Whittingham-led team, but it’s not surprising at this point, as stuff like this has been happening all year long.

Kellen: My biggest takeaway is that we learned that Tommy Carr is a good enough quarterback to make up for mediocre play calling.

Grace: Tommy Carr made some great plays and I think Michigan decided to establish some sort of passing identity. The receivers and tight ends made some plays, and it’s a good sign Michigan was able to score a few touchdowns. I’m still nervous about the inability to run the ball, especially given the teams remaining on Michigan’s schedule.

Matt: We didn’t learn much, but the offense’s inability to run the ball against arguably the worst rushing defense in the country is concerning. Don’t let the 161 rushing yards fool you — a large portion of those were Tommy Carr scrambles on broken plays. Michigan’s offense still has severe flaws and the Rutgers game didn’t do anything to assuage those fears.

Scotty: Tommy Carr looked great. Yes, it was Rutgers, but that was his second start. Great to see. On the flip side, I have no idea how this team manages to keep games like that close. Very concerning.

Charles: The offense still has a very, very long way to go to be competent, but it did show progress and seems to be operating at a higher level with Tommy Carr. The freshman quarterback was a real bright spot in his second career start and should continue to get better. Unfortunately, the defense uncharacteristically gave up a few big plays, and Trey Butkowski missed two field goals for a second straight week, so Rutgers was able to keep it close. In order to finish the season on a positive note, Michigan has to find a way to play well in all three phases, which hasn’t happened all season.

Now let’s talk about Michigan vs MSU, which will air at 7:30 p.m. on Peacock (sounds appropriate). Kyle Whittingham outright said this isn’t the most important rivalry game for the Wolverines. But how important is this game to you, even if it’s a lost season for both teams?

Von: I still obviously would love to see Michigan beat Michigan State for a fifth straight year, but it does feel a little different this season given how both teams have been playing and that they both have first-year head coaches that are just about to get a taste of what this rivalry is all about. I’m not saying it feels odd enough to the point where I wouldn’t be bummed out if Michigan lost — I definitely would be — but given how the season has gone for both teams, it does feel a bit like 2024 where a win would feel a little good and give you something to hold onto for another year, but it wouldn’t feel great like how some of the wins during the Harbaugh era did.

Kellen: This game is so important to me, for bragging rights and a general barometer of success for the season. I was in a terrible mood when we were visiting my aunt in Toledo in 2021 because of the Kenneth Walker game. I almost didn’t want to go to my high school’s homecoming dance my junior year because I watched the Trouble With The Snap with two MSU fans. And this game matters even more in a game like this, when both teams are the football equivalent of the cut-in-half donut that’s been sitting in your office’s conference room since 8 a.m.

Grace: It’s such a bummer to lose to Michigan State. While they haven’t looked the same in the rivalry since losing Mark Dantonio, it’s still a game you want to win. This season, Michigan State might not have the talent on its roster, but it’s not lost on me how head coach Pat Fitzgerald is able to scheme his way around that. This game always makes me nervous because there have only been a few times in memory that it hasn’t been a close one. Michigan State always plays up for this game.

Matt: In a world where the season is already over for all intents and purposes, I at least want to be able to hold it over a rival’s head that we can still beat them even when we stink. A win won’t do much for me but a loss would still be crushing.

Scotty: This game is always extremely important. Just because it isn’t the Ohio State game doesn’t mean it isn’t a massive game every season with a ton on the line no matter what. Michigan needs to win this game.

Charles: Kyle Whittingham was technically right with what he said, stating the Michigan State rivalry is important but there’s an even bigger one on the horizon against Ohio State. What he said was true, but it’s not something he should have said because he downplayed a rivalry, which sends a bad message to the team and fans. This rivalry is always going to be one of the biggest games of the season, no matter what the records say. In a year like this, its importance is even more magnified because both programs are desperately searching for season-defining wins, and this game is an opportunity.

Michigan has played up and down to their opponent’s talent level nearly every week this year. Is there any risk of that in a rivalry game, or does the rivalry itself solve that potential issue?

Von: It is kinda weird, right? Michigan narrowly beats WMU in Week 1, then beats a ranked SEC team in Oklahoma the very next week, then plays with its food and loses to Minnesota, and then plays close against Indiana before letting Rutgers stick around for way longer than it should have. This is the most up-and-down Michigan football team I have seen since covering the program. To answer the question, that definitely could happen in this rivalry game. I don’t think the Wolverines respect the Spartans the way they should. Savion Hiter calling it a “dirty” rivalry game is all I needed to hear, but Kyle Whittingham saying this game isn’t the most important rivalry game solidified it for me. Michigan cannot overlook this MSU team, because that is exactly how the Mark Dantonio era teams began beating Michigan until Harbaugh came around.

Kellen: I do think the players will get up for this game, being that they seem to have better understanding of the importance of this rivalry than the coaching staff. That said, I don’t think Michigan’s offense executes at a level it is capable of blowing out anyone in the Big Ten. I mean come on, the Wolverines almost just lost to RUTGERS, who got blown out by freaking UMass to start this troll’s paradise of a college football season. To match the 2007 vibes of this season, it feels appropriate for this game to be close.

Grace: I don’t expect the Wolverines to come out ready to play in a rivalry game like this. Actually, I worry they may keep some drives alive for Michigan State with some costly unsportsmanlike conduct penalties (even if they feel like soft calls). If you can’t beat Michigan State, bowl eligibility seems even further out of reach. Even if the team doesn’t care about playing in a non-playoff postseason game, maybe they care about not finishing with a losing record.

Matt: There certainly is risk of Michigan playing down to Michigan State’s level. Rutgers lost to UMass and Michigan only beat them by seven. In addition, who knows how chippy the game will be with two brand new coaches squaring off for the first time?

Scotty: I think there is a lot of risk of that happening this week. Michigan has a coach with little energy, and despite having more talent, I worry that Michigan State playing with more fire keeps it close. You don’t want to let an underdog hang around in a rivalry game.

Charles: I think Michigan will be more than motivated to beat Michigan State. However, that doesn’t mean it won’t be a close game. Michigan State has a tendency to stay within striking distance throughout the first half and into the second half before Michigan begins to pull away, and I expect that to be the case again.

Give us a bold prediction for tomorrow’s game.

Von: Michigan trails in the fourth quarter only to come back and barely squeak this one out.

Kellen: Tariq Boney scores on a scoop and score for the first touchdown of the game.

Grace: Michigan loses the turnover battle.

Matt: Tommy Carr leads Michigan in rushing with 75 yards and a touchdown.

Scotty: Michigan is favored in this game, so my bold prediction is that Michigan State will win.

Charles: Carr continues to carve out a legacy with a great performance against Michigan State, exceeding 300 total yards for a second straight week. Additionally, JJ Buchanan goes off for 100+ receiving yards, John Henry Daley and Dom Nichols return from injury and each get a sack, and Michigan’s defense forces multiple turnovers and holds Michigan State to less than 100 rushing yards.

What’s the final score and why?

Von (4-4): Michigan 20, MSU 17. The Wolverines kick a last-second field goal to barely win and keep Paul Bunyan in Ann Arbor.

Kellen (5-3): Michigan wins, 24-14. The defense is good enough to limit a crappy MSU team, but the offense isn’t nearly good enough to put the game away.

Grace (5-3): 17-7, Michigan. Michigan is able to move the ball on two drives, but stalls out or turns the ball over. The defense forces a late turnover and Trey Butkowski redeems himself from the past two games by kicking a late field goal to put the game out of reach for Michigan State.

Matt: (5-1): Michigan 17, Michigan State 7. Michigan’s defense should be back to its excellent, usual self. Carr and the pass game will do just enough, despite there being no run game whatsoever.

Scotty (1-4): 20-17, Michigan State. Michigan State is struggling, but at least Fitzgerald shows some passion. He’ll have them playing motivated in this game and I just don’t see Whittingham bringing that same energy to his team unfortunately.

Charles (4-2): I’ll pick Michigan, 24-13. Both teams trade blows in the first half, but the Wolverines settle in and create separation in the second half behind a stout defensive performance and another impressive showing from Carr. Michigan secures a fifth straight win in the rivalry and secures bowl eligibility.

michigan.headline: Fee Fi Foe Film: Michigan State Offense 2026
michigan.body:
Fee Fi Foe Film: Michigan State Offense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 5th, 2026 at 5:54 PM

[CONTENT NOTE: Jaziun Patterson, Marvis Parrish, and Jayden Savoury have both been ruled out for the game. This piece was written before that and could not be updated in time to compensate for the magnitude of those changes.]
The embattled Michigan State Spartans come to to Ann Arbor on Saturday to take on the hated Michigan Wolverines. It will be the first edition of this rivalry to pit Kyle Whittingham against Pat Fitzgerald and I can't say that either team is feeling too great about their season. Michigan fans are well versed on the predicament of this campaign and what it's been for the Maize & Blue, but Sparty is feeling morose as well. After starting 2-0, State has lost six in a row and a slew of injuries have limited much opportunity for improvement the rest of the season. Do they have enough in the tank to beat Michigan in a game MSU always gets up for? Let's begin to find out:

The Film: I wanted to watch MSU against a good defense as a comparison to Michigan, but also it had to be recent enough that the injury picture reflects the present. But not too recent, because starting QB Alessio Milivojevic missed MSU's previous game (they were on bye last week) with injury. That ruled out the UCLA game and Illinois' defense is far worse than Michigan's so they were off the list too. So, my options were really between Wisconsin and Northwestern, both of them pretty good defenses, and I went with the Northwestern game, purely for recency (played in mid-October).
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

One reason for optimism coming into MSU's season was the progression made by starting QB Alessio Milivojevic at the end of last season. It was in this rivalry game a year ago that Milivojevic began to see his workload increase and the Aidan Chiles era in East Lansing come to an end. Before long Milivojevic was starting games and was productive to end the season. This season has been okay from the inexperienced QB, putting together some nice performances and some iffier ones, with the game I charted being more in the latter category. I don't think Milivojevic is bad, but he's not actually good yet either.
The other reason for optimism was the addition of RB Cam Edwards from UConn, who was a Dude for the Huskies a year ago. The early returns for Edwards in a Spartan uniform were looking positive and then Edwards went down with an ACL injury against Nebraska, ending his season. The loss of Edwards leaves a hole at the RB position, with Iowa transfer Jaziun Patterson and WKU transfer Marvis Parrish attempting to fill it (Kenneth Williams is a seldom-used and subpar RB3). Patterson I like more than Parrish but I still think not having Edwards is a big loss for this group and further deprives them of skill position talent.
Largely because the WR situation is quite grim. I flagged it before the season as an area for concern and it remains generously a group of "just guys". A quick way to convey how that's the case is by speaking the words "starting WR Fred Moore" and then specifying that it's the same Fred Moore from Michigan. He's one of the starting wideouts, along with Rodney Bullard (originally a Valdosta State transfer) and slot Crishon McCray (originally a Kent State transfer). They are performing exactly how you would expect players from those schools to perform in the B1G. Sophomore Bryson Williams is the #4 WR and then there's a steep drop off in snaps from there. Not a lot of juice here.
At tight end, MSU is leaning heavily on Jaden Savoury and Brennan Parachek, while playing in a fair bit of 12 personnel this year. Savoury is a 6'5/253 lb. sophomore who does a lot of blocking and does serve as a receiver, usually into the flats or on other pedestrian routes. Paracheck is older, a one-time solid recruit out of Dexter who took a little bit of time to develop. He isn't much of a threat of a receiving target as Savoury but let's also not act like Savoury is Colston Loveland. It is a lot of mid that Milivojevic has to throw to this season.
The offensive line looked like it was in potentially solid shape coming into the year and I think that has mostly held up. We have seen some bad MSU lines over the years and this is far from that. It's not a fortress but they've stayed mostly heavy and rank in the top 50 of both PFF's team pass pro and team run blocking grades. UConn transfer LT Ben Murawski missed the Northwestern game that I charted but has been the consistent starter at that position in all the other games. In his place, Georgia Southern transfer Robert Wright Jr. started at RT and slid Rakeem Johnson over to LT. The tackles looked a bit weaker than the interior line to me on both the ground and in pass pro, where there were some wobbles.
The interior is pretty solid, though. I was excited about C Trent Fraley from North Dakota State in the offseason, as Fraley was a stand-out lineman in the FCS and he's translated into being a superb starting B1G C. That's the best player on the line, but the whole IOL did solid work in the game I charted, LG Conner Moore and RG Nick Sharpe (South Carolina transfer). Sharpe was banged up in the Northwestern game and was relieved by Luka Vincic, an Oregon State transfer who was one of Jonathan Smith's guys originally, and he was a bit of a step down. But no cyans on the OL for MSU for the first time in what feels like ages.

The TE flexed out plenty too:

I will be interested to see how ready Jay Hill's defense is to defend against the parts of the game when MSU picks up the pace.

Quarterback Dilithium Rating (Scale: 1 [Navarre] to 10 [Denard]): Alessio Milivojevic hasn't been a prolific rusher so far in his college football career, having rushed 24 times this season in seven games for a total of 106 yards in PFF's numbers (excluding sacks). That comes out to about 3.5 times per game for 4.4 per carry. Nothing particularly threatening. Milivojevic isn't slow or stiff really, it just isn't a focal point of how he approaches the QB position. The game I charted was actually Milivojevic's best game of the season running the ball, with six carries for 29 yards and he displayed a comfortability scrambling when the moment presented itself:

I liked the way Milivojevic shouldered contact and fought for extra yards on that play. He also is given the occasional opportunity to run the ball off reads, like this one from the first drive of the game:

Milivojevic moves around in the pocket some too, making a throw on the run here that was somewhat notable from the Illinois game:

It's nothing to scare you or be a bolded point on the scouting report, but Milivojevic isn't a statue. We'll go with a modest 4 here on our scale.
Dangerman: The Dangerman designation on offense is almost always reserved for a skill position player (I think I gave it to Iowa C Tyler Linderbaum once in the dredges of the Brian Ferentz era but otherwise), which put me in a pickle here because I am not all that enthused about any of the skill guys. RB Cam Edwards was the slam dunk pick when I was watching MSU during the season's first couple of weeks but with him out for the year with injury, I had to go with his backup, Jaziun Patterson.
An Iowa transfer, Patterson found himself trapped behind Kamari Moulton and looked elsewhere for a larger workload. With Edwards injured, Patterson is now the guy at RB for the Spartans and currently has 327 rushing yards on 76 carries this season, with five touchdowns to his name and a 4.3 YPC clip to boot. The performance against Northwestern was unremarkable, 72 yards on 15 carries for a 4.8 YPC (not awful) but a long of 12. It was a pretty pedestrian, but efficient day on the ground for Patterson, with runs like this comprising much of his day:

That's not exciting, but stuff like this from other games is:

There was also this rushing TD from the Illinois game, where Patterson just gets the ball across the goal line before it was punched out:

Patterson isn't much of a threat in the pass game, averaging one catch a game for 6.7 yards per reception. Mostly it's a checkdown option on passing plays where he isn't asked to help in blitz pickups, so you're really looking at him on the ground. When the blocking is good, Patterson can have some fun moments like in the 3 TD game vs. Illinois. He's not a game-breaker, but on this team and its lackluster skill position situation, he's the closest thing we have to a Dangerman.

That was two weeks ago, with the bye week in between, and Milivojevic was questionable in that game, being scratched before kickoff. I saw no information on any injury when I was looking around earlier, so my assumption is that Milivojevic is healthy and ready to go for the Michigan game. In any event, I wouldn't have much to say about the backups who faced UCLA (Leo Hannan/Kayd Coffman) anyway, other than "bad!".

He has thrown for 7 TDs and 3 INTs, two of the three coming in the Notre Dame game against the best defense that he's seen this season. 69% (nice) is not a bad DSR all things considered, but what stuck out to me is not what Milivojevic was able to accomplish but what he narrowly missed out on. The good stuff he did was ordinary and the bad stuff, if just a few plays were reversed, would've changed everything with this game. The meat left on the bone was tantalizing, as Milivojevic twice had an open receiver running free downfield and overthrew him. Here's one:

Those were two possible touchdowns, one on a drive that ended in a punt and the other on a 4th & 2, that Milivojevic couldn't get to his intended receivers. Fliip one of those two around and MSU wins. Flip both around and they win easily. That was the meat on the bone that was agonizing if you were a Spartan fan, where Milivojevic's arm just wasn't accurate enough. That's the biggest issue that I identified in the QB's game, as his decisions were generally fine. He makes a bad decision to throw this ball under pressure, though:

But the accuracy is an issue. On the big ones, it was overthrowing, but he also underthrew a deep shot (that was caught) on a different pass attempt. The arm talent is holding Milivojevic back (and I don't think he's terribly advanced as a processor yet), but we shouldn't all focus on the bad. He's been better than some of the QBs the Spartans cycled through during the late Mel Tucker/Jonathan Smith eras IMO and has had some nice games. Against Illinois' bad defense, Milivojevic went 22/26 for 196 and 2 TD (no turnovers), making throws like this:

And if we just focus on the Northwestern game that I charted, there were moments too. A lot of the throws he was asked to make were simple hitches and out routes, but this seam shot to Fred Moore gained 29:

Milivojevic feels like a decent college QB right now, nothing more than that. He's by far the best option they have based on the performance of the backups but he's also probably not ready for primetime as the Notre Dame game showed. One example:

I don't think Milivojevic will have the best game against a very good Michigan defense on Saturday in Ann Arbor, but he's only a junior and a first year starter. There are some skills to work with moving forward for Pat Fitzgerald's staff, but right now Milivojevic is in the middle pack of the conference as a QB.

Overview
As Michigan State rolls into the first Saturday in November, the Spartans have the nation's #97 offense per SP+. That number presumably is a bit artificially low due to the UCLA game, where the Milivojevic-less Spartans mustered only a feeble 156 yards on 2.9 yards per play. There have been better performances against other teams when their starting QB was playing and the Northwestern game was probably MSU's best showing of the season adjusting for opponent. But I don't want to get too out over my skis with optimism when the Spartan offense put up 10 points against Notre Dame, 13 against Nebraska, and 3 against Wisconsin.
When we look towards the Michigan game and the matchup with the Wolverines' 4th ranked defense, we have to be realistic about the limitations here for State. It's going to be an uphill climb and for me the biggest issue is the most obvious one: a lack of talent. The skill position problems I mentioned in the Dangerman section are huge limiting factors. They just don't have enough good players to threaten a high-end opposing defense. Even looking at a team like Rutgers, there sure as hell isn't a KJ Duff on this MSU squad.
The receiver room is among the worst in the B1G, gutted by years of coaching turnover and recruiting troubles. When you're starting Fred Moore, you're in real trouble, as we Michigan fans know. The starting trio of Moore, Crishon McCray, and Rodney Bullard is lacking in oomph, as you'd expect for a trio that consists of a Valdosta State transfer, a Kent State transfer, and a guy who was not B1G caliber at Michigan. Of those three, I like McCray the most, having shown some ability to make plays in the tape I've reviewed. He ran down the seam and then broke a tackle for a TD against Northwestern:

Statistically speaking it's McCray leading the way on the team with 289 yards on 29 catches for 10 YPC, with that clip being his lone TD. Bullard and Moore have 21 and 20 catches, respectively, for between 210 and 260 yards and a combined three touchdowns. It's very meager across the board. As I mentioned with Milivojevic, most of the throws that MSU is attempting aren't that dangerous. Some of that is Milivojevic's accuracy and some of that is they don't have game breaking players to run down the field in the pass game. So you get a pass game that isn't threatening the opponent's defense much and attempting plays like this:

That limits what you can accomplish in the pass game and also allows safeties to play more rolled down in the run game. That was most of the problem in my eyes with the run game against Northwester. The blocking up front was acceptable, but MSU wasn't able to break any explosives. I am a big fan of C Trent Fraley but even when he and one of the guards were clearing open lanes, it was for modest gains, and not big time plays:

The interior line is a nice group on the ground and in pass protection, while the tackles are weaker. They aren't liabilities, but pass protection wobbles were extant against Northwestern:

That rush was around Rakeem Johnson, who is normally at RT but was playing LT in this game due to an injury to Ben Murawski. That meant Robert Wright had to play RT and he wasn't great. Still, it wasn't an all-out siege of Milivojevic. He had the time necessary to win the game with a few better throws. I assume Michigan's DL will have their wins even against the starting OL (Notre Dame had four sacks, Nebraska had six) but I don't think it will be an every down assault. This OL is better than the turnstiles of MSU OLines in the past.
Are there any other components to talk about with this offense? The main one I'd offer is tight end, where Jadyen Savoury is the other key receiving target. His catches have gone for an average of 9.3 yards this season and isn't a player that I fear a mismatch with. Most of what is thrown his way is stuff like this:

Between Savoury, Moore, Bullard, and McCray, the receiving targets are a whole bunch of mid.

What does this mean for Michigan?
I don't think MSU's offense is as broken of a unit as you would think based on its SP+ ranking, but it remains untalented. That's the crux of the problem. They have a really good center and that's about it. A solid starting RB (who was supposed to be the backup), an average B1G QB with accuracy limitations, a middling line, and one of the worst receiver groups in the B1G (maybe the worst). There is coherence to what they want to do and against lesser defenses, it can work. They scored a lot against Illinois and I presume they'll have a good day in the final week of the season against Rutgers.
But against a defense like Michigan's, I am not sure there's a pathway here. Michigan's DL should be able to get some pressure on Milivojevic and keep the run game in check. And if that's the case, there are no receivers like Chase Sowell or Tony Diaz or KJ Duff or Charlie Becker or Nick Marsh to challenge Michigan's DBs. I would expect this to look like it did against Notre Dame (10 points, 3.7 YPP) or Wisconsin (3 points, 3.0 YPP), an unproductive evening that likely won't be enough to put MSU over the top even if their defense handles the Wolverine offense well.

ANN ARBOR, MI - OCTOBER 24: Michigan Wolverines wide receiver Andrew Marsh (3) looks on at the conclusion of a regular season Big Ten Conference college football game between the Indiana Hoosiers and the Michigan Wolverines on October 24, 2026 at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Heading into the regular season both the Michigan Wolverines and the Michigan State Spartans brought new head coaches into the fold. Neither Kyle Whittingham nor Pat Fitzgerald have had the opening year that they anticipated since then.

Now, they battle for the first time as rivals in a newfound era of hate between two schools 65 miles apart in the Mitten State.

Michigan Wolverines vs Michigan State Spartans

Day: Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026

TV: Peacock

Time: 7:30 p.m. ET

Location: Ann Arbor, MI

Weather: 44 degrees, partly cloudy

Odds: MICH – 13.5, O/U: 39.5

We’ve resorted to the Michigan Wolverines not even being on network television this weekend against their second biggest rival, the in-state Spartans. Woof.

Neither Whittingham nor Fitzgerald have figured out how to run an offense in the Big Ten this year. Michigan is 119th in yards and 106th in points per game while Michigan State is 129th and 112th in the same categories. Football fans in this great state have seen porous offense and little success.

The Wolverines at least have found a way to win, going 5-3 so far this year and beating Rutgers and Penn State to be in a place of bowl eligibility. Michigan State is 2-6, one of two teams winless in the conference, and only topping Toledo and Eastern Michigan in their first two contests.

Where I have to credit the Spartans is how they’ve performed at home. They lost by a combined four points to Illinois and a ranked Northwestern team. Unfortunately for them, this one is in Ann Arbor, and they have been horrible on the road this year and Michigan State is down to their third quarterback.

Alessio Milivojevic missed last weeks contest against UCLA, QB2 Cam Fancher is also injured, leading to true freshman Kayd Coffman going 4-for-10 with a TD and a pick against UCLA in the Rose Bowl last weekend. The general sentiment based on comments heading into Saturday is Milivojevic could be out again in their most important game of the year at the Big House. It doesn’t stop there, either; three injuries in the running back room and several in the secondary leave the Spartans severely banged up heading into the Battle for Paul Bunyan.

Michigan simply cannot lost this football game. Last week, they went down to the fourth quarter against a bad Rutgers football team in New Jersey. With the injuries that the Spartans are operating through, they may be even worse.

That being said, Pat Fitzgerald has put much more of an emphasis on this game then Whittingham has, which should be a concern. At Big Ten media days, the former Northwestern football player and coach talked about how much he loved beating Michigan. In April, he was counting down the days until this matchup. And this week made this comment, “This is a week that not only our players, our staff but all of our fans, our alums, our former players circle.”

Meanwhile, Whittingham has continuously underplayed the rivalries against both Ohio State and Michigan State. Earlier this week, it sounded like he heard about the tunnel fight for the first time. Who know the kinds of juice his team is going to come out with after everything that has already happened this year.

Two horrible offenses makes me think that this game will go chalk with what has happened historically in this rivalry. In 49 of the last 56 matchups, the team with more rushing yards won the Paul Bunyan Trophy. The total here is low for a reason, and I just don’t see Michigan in a position to win by multiple scores and pull away. They haven’t proven they can do it against competition with a pulse this year. I think the Wolverines win, but it’s not by two scores.

On Wednesday night, the Michigan State Men’s Soccer Team wrapped up their regular season.  In the season finale, the Spartans fell at Indiana.  The Hoosiers clinched the Big Ten regular season crown with the win.  MSU still had a fine season, finishing with a 5-3-2 conference record and a 10-4-3 overall mark, good for 4th place in the conference.  Just like the women’s side, the top eight teams qualify for the Big Ten Tournament, meaning our team will have a chance to win more games and perhaps even qualify for the NCAA Tournament.

Across 17 games, MSU outscored their opponents, 36-22.  The scoring was more spread out than the women, with only Andrew Darakdjian surpassing 5 goals, finishing at 8.  11 other players accounted for the remaining 28 scores.  Jake Grekowicz is the guy in net.  He started all 17 games on the season and tallied a 1.30 GAA.  He had 6 shutouts.

Looking ahead to the BTT, the Spartans will face the 5-seed Maryland in their opener.  That game will be on Sunday, November 8, at 1 PM, and will air on BTN+.  The two teams collided on October 9 when MSU went to College Park and picked up a 2-1 win.  This game will be at 1-seed Indiana University, and if we advance, that will be the location of our semifinal game as well.  The tournament finals will be at the home of the highest remaining seed.

Let’s go Spartans!

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The um wolverines
msu.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches practice at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor ahead of the game between Michigan and Oklahoma on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation.  This column has been away for a few weeks with a bye last week and the game against UCLA before that, which does not have an SB Nation site.  But we are back for our in-state hate game.  I sat down with Von Lozon of Maize N Brew for a quick look at this weekend’s opponent.  Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: UM is in the first year under head coach Kyle Whittingham. Did that hire take you by surprise? Aside from any surprise, what were your thoughts on the hire? What were your expectations for this season in terms of performance and record?

Von Lozon:  I wasn’t surprised, but I was skeptical of the hire simply due to his age and me wondering how much he had left in the tank. I never thought he was a bad coach or anything like that — if anything, I thought he was one of the more underrated coaches in the country — but I was a little nervous about how things would translate at Michigan and in the Big Ten. I thought this team’s ceiling heading into the year was 9-3, which they can still technically reach, but I would be incredibly shocked if that happened.

TOC: Your season opener came down to a famously controversial ending. I won’t ask you for your thoughts on how that played out. But I would like to know how much panic you had after that first game? After that 1st game, UM was expected to lose their 2nd game against Oklahoma. How did that win reshape your expectations?

VL: Given my offseason skepticism, I was really worried following the WMU game. But then the Wolverines beat Oklahoma the very next week and I was thinking to myself, “Okay, maybe that is more of what we should expect.” And then the next week, Michigan was in a first-half dog fight against UTEP, so at that point, I knew this would be a team that plays up (and down) to its competition. That has continued every week all season, as the only game that wasn’t a one-score affair was that UTEP game. Needless to say, it’s been a roller coaster of a year for Michigan.

TOC: Whittingham has made a switch at QB, with Tommy Carr taking over a couple games ago as the starter. What do you think went wrong with Bryce Underwood? Should the switch have been made sooner? What do you like about Carr’s game that makes him better than Underwood?

VL: It’s a really curious case, right? Underwood flashed his potential at times during his freshman season, but he looked even more lost this year before the coaching staff made the change. It’s interesting, especially considering all the reports coming out of fall camp were that Underwood had improved under the new coaching staff’s direction and should take a sophomore leap. But his freshman tendencies (staring down one receiver, bailing out of the pocket too soon, etc.) came back to haunt him this season, resulting in far too many negative plays and turnovers.

I do think the switch should have been made during the game at Minnesota, but admittedly, that would have been a really tough spot to put a freshman quarterback in the game for the first time. The thing I like so far about Carr is his poise. He hasn’t let anything phase him too much yet — even though he struggled at the start of the Indiana game with a couple of turnovers, he kept his head down, kept working and eventually put Michigan in a good position to win (thanks a lot, Jason Beck!).

TOC: Tell us about the Wolverine defense. What is the base formation? What level of the D is the best? What player do the MSU coaches most need to game plan for?

VL: The defense is by far the best part of this football team. Jay Hill runs a true 4-3 defensive scheme with the linebackers playing off the ball. The wrinkle is that one of the linebackers can be a bit of a hybrid player at times. Depending on the call, that linebacker can be up on the line of scrimmage setting the edge or dropping into the box. It gives Michigan’s defense some flexibility without needing to change personnel. Look for Chase Taylor (No. 4), who has been in this role quite a bit this year, as well as MIKE linebacker Troy Bowles (No. 18).
The best level of the defense is the defensive line. Michigan can rotate edge rushers like John Henry Daley, Dom Nichols, Nate Marshall, Benny Patterson III, and true freshmen Tariq Boney and Carter Meadows without a real drop-off. The interior group of Trey Pierce, Enow Etta and Jonah Lea’ea has been solid as well. That depth lets them stay fresh and keep the pressure on for four quarters.

The player MSU needs to game plan for is Daley. He missed last week’s game due to an injury, but he is expected to play this weekend. He leads the team in sacks (4) and also has 6.5 tackles for loss. When he has been on the field, he has been Michigan’s best edge rusher. Nichols is right behind him, and the two of them together are why the defense can get to the quarterback so often without blitzing.

TOC: Fill in the blank: UM will win if ___________.  UM will lose if ___________.

VL: U-M will win if they avoid turning the ball over, run the ball well (AKA: go on long drives that drain the clock), and score touchdowns, not field goals, in the red zone.

U-M will lose if they turn the ball over, give up some explosive plays to MSU’s offense (much like vs Rutgers last week), and take MSU lightly. On that last point, I’m a little worried these guys don’t really know a whole lot about this rivalry. Kyle Whittingham has said multiple times that this game is important, but it isn’t the most important rivalry game Michigan has. Savion Hiter said all he knows about this game is that the rivalry is “dirty.” I really have not enjoyed hearing the things that some of these guys have said throughout the week, so I really, really hope Michigan doesn’t take MSU for granted.

TOC: Predict the final score.

VL: Michigan 20, Michigan State 17.
